text: • HACEK endocarditis. The HACEK organisms are slow and difficult to culture and treatment must often, therefore, be empirical. Traditionally, treatment for this group of organisms was based on ampicillin and gen- tamicin. However, because of the emergence of beta- lactamase producing strains, empirical treatment is now based on beta-lactamase-stable cephalosporins. Preferred treatment for native-valve endocarditis due to HACEK organisms is therefore with intramuscular or intravenous ceftriaxone (usually in a dose of 2 g once daily) for 4 weeks,4,6-8 although cefotaxime4 or other third-generation cephalosporin may be used instead. UK guidelines recommend addition of gentamicin for the first 2 weeks of therapy.6 Alternatively, if the isolate is penicillin sensitive, ampicillin plus 2 weeks of gen- tamicin,6 or ampicillin-sulbactam8 have been suggested. US guidelines consider that a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin for 4 weeks, by mouth or intravenously, may also be effective.8 • Endocarditis due to other organisms. Treatment of endocarditis due to other organisms depends greatly on the organism and its susceptibility; early surgery is often required. For endocarditis due to Pseudomonas spp. a combination of an antipseudomonal beta-lactam with tobramycin has been suggested.5,7 Endocarditis associ- ated with the intracellular pathogen Coxiella burnetii re- quires very prolonged therapy with doxycycline,6,7 in combination with rifampicin7 or a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin.6 Regimens suggested for Bartonella endocarditis have included a penicillin or ceftriaxone in combination with gentamicin, or doxycycline plus gen- tamicin.6,8 For other potential causes of culture-negative endocarditis, empirical treatment with a penicillin or vancomycin plus gentamicin, sometimes in combina- tion with a third antibiotic such as rifampicin or cipro- floxacin, has been suggested.4,7,8 Endocarditis prophylaxis. Because of the potentially severe consequences of endo- carditis, prophylaxis is widely practised in patients consid- ered to be at increased risk when they are exposed to pro- cedures likely to produce bacteraemia, although much of the evidence to support the practice is circumstantial and the benefits and risks therefore hard to calculate.
